title: React at Scale: Performance, State, TypeScript

scenes.say: You type one letter, and ten thousand rows redraw. A hundred twenty milliseconds, every keystroke. By the end you'll cut that to about two, and type your components so bugs fail at compile time.
Today you will do three things. Skip wasted renders, and draw only the rows on screen. Decide where shared state lives. And type your components so mistakes fail at compile time.
lines: Skip wasted renders, draw only visible rows
Type components so bugs fail to compile

scenes.title: Laggy search box
scenes.statement: A search box sits above a list of 10,000 rows. Each key you type re-renders every row: 120 ms in the profiler.
scenes.say: Type one letter, and the list should answer in about two milliseconds. Today the profiler says a hundred twenty.

scenes.head: The re-grading teacher
scenes.say: Picture a teacher with thirty papers. One student changes an answer. A bad teacher re-grades all thirty. A good teacher re-grades only that one. Memo is the good one.

scenes.head: Type a letter: every row renders
scenes.say: Here is what happens. App holds the text you type. Under it sit ten thousand rows. You type a. App re-renders, and so do all the rows, though they did not change. The profiler says a hundred twenty milliseconds. Type b, and it happens again.

scenes.head: Fix one: React.memo + useCallback
scenes.say: Fix one: React dot memo wraps the list. It compares props, and skips the list if they match. Every key you type changes q, but the list props stay the same. The catch: a function written inside App is a new function every render. Use callback keeps one.
Your turn. Rows is wrapped in memo, but now it gets an inline arrow function as on pick. You type a letter. Does React skip Rows? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `<Rows onPick={(id) => go(id)} />` in memo. Skipped on a keystroke?

scenes.head: Inline function: memo is bypassed
scenes.say: No. An inline function is a new function on every render, so the props compare as changed, and all rows render again: a hundred twenty. Wrap it in use callback, and the props match. Rows is skipped, and the cost drops to zero.

scenes.title: 10,000 rows that really change
scenes.statement: The filter still matches all 10,000 rows, and each keystroke makes a new array, so memo cannot skip them.
scenes.say: Memo has one weakness: it skips only when props match. Suppose the filter still matches ten thousand rows. Can we hit about two milliseconds?

scenes.head: Virtualization: a window on the list
scenes.say: Picture a scroll of paper seen through a small window. A list is the scroll, and your screen is the window. So why build ten thousand rows? Virtualization draws only the visible ones, plus a few spare. Scroll to the middle: rows four thousand on. The cost: two milliseconds.

scenes.head: Libraries and useMemo
scenes.say: You rarely write the swapping yourself. React window and Tan Stack Virtual do it. Use memo is a different tool. It caches a computed value, here the filtered list, and recomputes only when items or q change. Memo skips a render. Use memo skips a calculation.
Quick check. The filter sits in use memo, with items and q as its inputs. Now App re-renders, but only the theme changed. Does the filter run again? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Deps `[items, q]`. App re-renders after only `theme` changes. Filter reruns?

scenes.head: Same inputs, cached answer
scenes.say: No. The inputs are items and q, and neither changed, so React hands back the cached list. Theme is not an input. Now type a letter. Q changes, so the filter runs again, and the new list is cached.

scenes.head: Mistakes interviewers listen for
scenes.say: Memo on everything? Comparing props costs too, so profile first. Use callback on a child that is not in memo does nothing. State held too high re-renders the page, so move it down. Array index as a key mixes up reordered rows, so use a stable id. And load routes lazily, so the first download stays small.
rows: move it next to the input
a stable id as the key

scenes.title: One cart, three components
scenes.statement: A header badge, a product list and a cart page all show the same cart. Where should the cart live?
scenes.say: Three components share one cart. One source of truth is the rule. The header says two. The cart page says three. Which one is right?

scenes.head: The list on the fridge door
scenes.say: Think of a family shopping list. If it lives in one person's head, nobody else can use it. Stick it on the fridge door, and everyone can read it. The kid adds bread, and everyone sees bread. A parent component is the fridge door.

scenes.head: Step 1: lift state up
scenes.say: Step one is the fridge door. The cart state moves up to Page, the closest common parent. Page passes the count down to Header. List gets an add function. Click add, and Page updates to one, and the badge shows one. Start here. Most apps need nothing more.

scenes.head: Step 2: prop drilling, then context
scenes.say: Now the badge sits deep: Page, Layout, Sidebar, Toolbar, Header. Layout, Sidebar and Toolbar never use the count, yet each must pass it along. That is prop drilling. Context skips the middle. Anything under a provider, a wrapper that hands the value down, reads the value directly.

scenes.head: Step 3: context, or a store
scenes.say: Wrap the tree in a provider, and Header reads the value with use context. But when the value changes, every consumer re-renders. Context suits slow values, like theme. For fast data, use an external store, like Zoostand or Redux. A component subscribes to just the slice it needs.
Your turn. One context holds the cart count and the theme. The theme flips. Header reads only the count. Does Header re-render? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Context value is `{ n, theme }`. Theme flips. Header reads only `n`.

scenes.head: Context vs a store slice
scenes.say: Yes. Context re-renders every consumer when its value changes, even one reading a single field. Memo does not stop it. So the context Header re-renders on every theme flip. With a store, Header reads only the count slice, so the theme flip skips it.

scenes.head: Where each kind of state lives
scenes.say: Use this table. Form input stays local, never global. Siblings sharing a value use the closest common parent. Slow app wide values, like theme, go in context. Fast shared state, like the cart, goes in a store. Server data goes in a query cache, like Tan Stack Query.

scenes.title: A typo that reaches users
scenes.statement: A page reads user.nmae by mistake. In plain JavaScript it ships, and customers see undefined.
scenes.say: It is Friday evening, and someone types user dot nmae. In plain JavaScript it ships, and customers see undefined. We want the compiler to stop it with an error.

scenes.head: The shipping label
scenes.say: Think of a shipping label. It says fragile, two kilos. That label is the type. The warehouse checks every parcel against its label. That is the compiler. But the delivered box has no label. Types are erased, so nothing is checked at runtime.

scenes.head: Type or interface?
scenes.say: The classic question. For object shapes they are almost the same. To extend, an interface says extends. A type uses an ampersand. Only a type can name a union or a tuple, a fixed-length list. Only interfaces support declaration merging, where same-name ones join. Rule: interface for objects, type for the rest.

scenes.head: Generics: a type placeholder
scenes.say: A generic is a type placeholder. Item of T is a box holding a value of type T. Item of string holds a pen. Item of number holds forty. And first takes an array of T and returns a T, or undefined if the list is empty. Pass numbers, T is number. Pass strings, T is string. One function, fully typed. Run it on Node twenty three point six or newer, or with tsx.

scenes.head: Narrowing with typeof
scenes.say: Narrowing means the compiler tracks what a value can be. Here x is a string or a number. Calling to fixed on it is an error. Check typeof first. Inside the if, x is a string. After the return, it must be a number. It prints five, then seven point zero.

scenes.head: Discriminated union
scenes.say: Objects narrow too. Give each shape a kind field with a literal value. That is a discriminated union. Check the kind. Inside the if, TypeScript knows it is a circle, so r is available. After the return, it must be a square, so w is available.
Your turn. User has an id and a name. Pick of User and id keeps only the id. Which value has that type? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: User is `{ id, name }`. Which value has type `Pick<User, 'id'>`?

scenes.head: Utility types reshape a type
scenes.say: Id three. Pick keeps only the id, so an object with a name is an excess property. That is an error on a literal. Utility types reshape a type for you. Partial makes every field optional, handy for an edit form. Pick keeps the fields you name. Omit drops them.

scenes.head: The trap: as silences the compiler
scenes.say: The trap. As tells the compiler to trust you. Here the data has no name, but as User says it does. It compiles, then throws, and the catch prints the crash. Types are erased, so nothing checks it. Fix it by validating at the boundary, with a library like zod. Or take unknown and narrow it. Never reach for any.

scenes.head: Optimize React?
scenes.say: How do you optimize React? Profile first, then memo, and virtualize big lists. useMemo or memo? useMemo caches a value. Memo skips a render. Memo everything? No, comparing props costs too. Where does useCallback fit? It keeps a function stable for a memo child. Common mistake? useCallback on a child that is not memoized.

scenes.head: Manage state?
scenes.say: How do you manage state? Keep it local, and lift it when siblings share. Context or store? Context for slow values, a store for fast ones. Do I need Redux? Rarely. Context covers most apps. Why does context re-render? Every consumer does, whenever the value changes. Server data? Use a query cache, not global state.
rows: Keep it local, and lift it when siblings share.
Context for slow values, a store for fast ones.
Rarely. Local state and context cover most apps.

scenes.say: Self-test. Out loud, in one sentence: what is the difference between any and unknown? Pause and answer.

scenes.head: Types or interfaces?
scenes.say: Type or interface? Interface for object shapes, a type for unions and tuples. Generics? A type parameter, inferred per call, keeps the return type exact. Narrowing? Check typeof, or a shared kind field, and the compiler narrows. Utility types? Partial makes fields optional. Pick and Omit keep or drop named fields.
rows: Interface for object shapes; a type for unions and tuples.
A type parameter, inferred per call, keeps the return type exact.

scenes.head: Types at runtime?
scenes.say: Are types checked at runtime? No. They are erased, so validate data with zod. Any versus unknown? Unknown forces a check before use, any turns checking off. Common mistake? Using as to silence errors instead of narrowing.

scenes.head: Try these before your interview
scenes.say: Three exercises. Render ten thousand rows in a list, profile it, then virtualize it. Move a cart count into a store, and read only that slice. And turn on strict mode in TypeScript, then replace one as with a real check.
rows: Profile a 10,000-row list, then virtualize it
Move a cart count into a Zustand store slice
Turn on `strict`, replace one `as` with a check

scenes.say: So say this. Profile first, then skip renders and virtualize big lists. Keep state low, lift it for siblings, and store fast data. Types vanish at runtime, so validate data at the edge.
lines: Profile first. Skip renders, virtualize lists.
Keep state low. Lift it, then context, then a store.
